annotations.keyFindings: Matched on diagnosis, age and frailty, 30-day readmission was 15.8 percent after hospital at home and 13.1 percent after ward care (adjusted odds ratio 1.12, CI 0.94 to 1.34); higher for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
annotations.limitations: One service; matching cannot remove selection into hospital at home; no reasons for readmission.

annotations.keyFindings: Carers took on night monitoring they felt untrained for and called ambulances when the night line felt slow; a written plan for night-time worsening was linked to fewer emergency calls.
annotations.limitations: Twenty-two carers from one service; no link to readmission records.

annotations.keyFindings: In trials, 90-day readmission after hospital at home was similar to ward care (risk ratio 1.05); few studies reported reasons for readmission or patient and carer views.
annotations.limitations: Selected trial populations; observational results heterogeneous.

annotations.keyFindings: Clinicians transferred patients back at lower thresholds at night, with unfamiliar patients and when day-night handovers lacked a shared plan for worsening.
annotations.limitations: Eighteen clinicians in three services; retrospective accounts.

annotations.keyFindings: Of 300 readmissions after hospital at home, 18 percent followed carer breakdown or social crisis and 34 percent were judged potentially avoidable (kappa 0.58 for avoidability).
annotations.limitations: One service; record-based judgements with moderate agreement.

annotations.keyFindings: Qualitative studies of care transitions with a narrow aim and a specific sample reported adequate information with 12 to 20 interviews per participant group.
annotations.limitations: Methods review; no fixed sample size rule.

claims.text: In a matched cohort, readmission within thirty days after hospital at home (15.8 percent) was not clearly different from ward care (13.1 percent) after adjustment (adjusted odds ratio 1.12).

claims.interpretation: The dashboard gap may partly reflect case mix; counting alone will not explain it.

claims.text: Family carers in a hospital-at-home service described calling an ambulance at night because the service's night line felt slow or because they did not want to disturb the team.
claims.passage: Several described calling an ambulance because the service's night line felt slow or because they did not want to disturb the team.
claims.interpretation: Carer decisions at night are a plausible route to readmission worth exploring locally.

claims.interpretation: Clinician escalation decisions need their own interviews, not only patient and carer accounts.

synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Readmission after hospital at home is similar to ward care in trials and not clearly different after matching in one cohort, so the local dashboard gap may partly reflect who is admitted. What the evidence does not explain is why patients return: carers describe night-time uncertainty and slow night lines, clinicians describe lower thresholds for transfer at night and weak handover plans, and a record review attributes a fifth of readmissions to carer breakdown and a third to potentially avoidable causes. These findings point to an explanatory question that interviews with patients, carers and clinicians can answer.
gradeRationale: Observational and small qualitative studies from single services, one systematic review of selected trials; consistent themes but indirect for this program.
summary: Six records appraised; five source-derived claims; overall certainty low.
